(p-197) Surah "Ghafir"

All the Ḥawāmīm (the surahs beginning with ḥā-mīm) are Meccan, related from Ibn ʿAbbās.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾. As for this and what follows it, Ḥamzah, ʿAlī, Khalaf, Yaḥyā and Ḥammād (may Allah have mercy on them) read it with imāla (inclination of the vowel toward i). Madanī read it with a pronunciation between fatḥa and kasra, while the others read it with tafkhīm (full, emphatic pronunciation). It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that it is the Greatest Name of Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 3:

﴿Forgiver of sin﴾, concealer of the sins of the believers,

﴿and Accepter of repentance﴾, accepter of the repentance of those who turn back (to Him),

﴿severe in punishment﴾, against those who oppose Him,

﴿Possessor of bounty﴾, possessor of favour upon those who know Him; or possessor of wealth free of need of all things. And from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): ﴿Forgiver of sin and Accepter of repentance﴾ is for the one who says: "There is no god but Allah," and ﴿severe in punishment﴾ is for the one who does not say: "There is no god but Allah."

"Al-tawb," "al-thawb," and "al-awb" are siblings in meaning of return (ruju'). "Al-tawl" means wealth (al-ghina) and favour (al-fadl).

(p-198) If you ask: how do these attributes differ in definiteness and indefiniteness, when the described (noun) is definite? I answer: as for "Forgiver of sin" and "Accepter of repentance," they are definite, because by them is not meant the occurrence of the two acts so that they would be in the sense of separation; thus their annexation is not a true (genuine) annexation. Rather, what is meant is the establishment and continuity of that. As for "severe in punishment," it is in the sense of "severe is His punishment," and so it is indefinite. It has been said: it is a substitute (badal). It has also been said: when this indefinite noun was found among these definite nouns, it indicated that all of them are substitutes, not attributes. The insertion of the waw in "and Accepter of repentance" is for a purpose, namely to convey that the sinner who repents combines two mercies: that He accepts his repentance and records it for him as one of the acts of obedience, and that He makes it an erasure of sins, as if he had never sinned. It is as if He said: "Gatherer of forgiveness and acceptance."

It is narrated that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) missed a man of great strength from the people of Syria, and it was said to him: "He persists in this drinking." 'Umar said to his scribe: "Write: From 'Umar to so-and-so, peace be upon you. I praise Allah to you, besides whom there is no god, [In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful] (Ha Mim), to His saying: ﴿to Him is the final return﴾." He sealed the letter and said to his messenger: "Do not hand it to him until you find him sober." Then he ordered those around him to pray for him to repent. When the letter reached him, he began to read it and say: "Allah has promised me that He will forgive me, and has warned me of His punishment." He did not cease repeating it until he wept. Then he pulled back (from sin), and he pulled back well, and his repentance was good. When 'Umar's report of him reached him, he said: "Do thus when you see your brother has slipped in a slip: correct him, support him, and pray to Allah that He accept his repentance, and do not be helpers of the devils against him."

﴿There is no god but He﴾, is also an attribute of ﴿Possessor of bounty﴾, and it may be that it is a new (independent) sentence.

﴿To Him is the final return﴾, the destination.

The Qur'anic quotations inside ﴿ ﴾ are rendered with their meaning. Here is the translation:

Surah 40 (Ghafir), verse 4, in al-Nasafi's Madarik al-Tanzil:

﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾. None contend about them by denying them and rejecting them, and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood in order to refute the truth thereby﴾ [Ghafir: 5]. As for disputing about them in order to clarify what is ambiguous in them, resolve what is difficult in them, derive their meanings, and refute the people of deviation by means of them, it is the greatest struggle (jihad) in the way of God.

﴿So let not their movement throughout the land deceive you﴾: that is, with profitable trade and lucrative gains, going about safe and laden with spoils. For indeed the end of their affair is toward punishment. Then he explained how this is, so he informed that the nations who denied before them were destroyed, and so He said:

The people of Nuh denied before them, Nuh,

﴿and the factions﴾, that is, those who formed factions against the messengers and opposed them, namely ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Lut, and others,

﴿after them﴾, after the people of Nuh,

﴿And every community plotted﴾, from among these nations, which are the people of Nuh and the factions,

﴿against their messenger to seize him﴾, to gain power over him and kill him. The *akhidh* (أخيذ) means the captive,

﴿and they disputed with falsehood﴾, with disbelief,

﴿to refute thereby the truth﴾, to nullify thereby the faith,

﴿So I seized them﴾. The reading is *muzhar* (مُظْهَرٌ, with the sound clearly articulated, *idhhar*), and it is the reading of Makki (Ibn Kathir) and Hafs. It means that they intended to seize him, so I made their punishment, in return for their intention to seize the messengers, that I seized them, that is, I punished them,

﴿So how was My punishment﴾. With *ya'* (بِالياءِ, the first person verb written with the letter ya), it is the reading of Yaʿqub, meaning: indeed you pass by their lands and witness the traces of that. This is an affirmation which carries the sense of wonder.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 6:

﴿And thus the word of your Lord has come true against those who disbelieved﴾, "كَلِماتُ رَبِّكَ" (kalimat rabbika, the plural "words of your Lord"), read by the people of Medina and Syria (Madani and Shami) as "كَلِمَتُ رَبِّكَ" (kalimat rabbika, singular "word of your Lord"),

﴿that they are the companions of the Fire﴾. It is in the place of nominative case (mahall al-raf'), as a substitute (badal) for "كَلِمَةِ رَبِّكَ" (kalimat rabbika). That is: like that decree, there became incumbent upon the disbelievers that they are among the companions of the Fire. Its meaning: just as their destruction in this world by a total punishment became incumbent, so too their destruction by the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter became incumbent. Or it is in the place of accusative case (mahall al-nasb), with the removal of the preposition of causation (lam al-ta'lil) and the connection of the verb (idsal al-fi'l), and "الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا" (alladhina kafaru, "those who disbelieved") refers to the Quraysh. Its meaning: just as the destruction of those earlier nations became incumbent, so too the destruction of these (p-200) became incumbent, because one single cause unites them: that they are among the companions of the Fire. And a pause (waqf) on "اَلنّارِ" (al-nar, "the Fire") is required, because if it were connected, it would become [a different meaning].

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 7:**

﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it﴾: meaning the bearers of the Throne and those who surround it, who are the Cherubim (al-Karubiyyun), the chiefs of the angels. It is a description (sifah) of the people of the Fire. Its incorrectness is evident. It is narrated that the bearers of the Throne have their feet in the lowest earth, and their heads have pierced the Throne, and they are in humility, not raising their gaze. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah (Exalted) commanded all the angels to go out and return with peace upon the bearers of the Throne, honouring them above the rest of the angels." It is said: around the Throne are seventy thousand rows of angels, standing with their hands placed on their shoulders, glorifying (yuhallilun) and magnifying (yukabbirun) God. Behind them are a hundred thousand rows who have placed their right hands on their left. None of them is there but glorifying God with something other than what the other glorifies.

﴿Glorifying﴾ (yusabbihun) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada'), which is "alladhina" (those who).

﴿with the praise of their Lord﴾: that is, together with His praise; or the preposition bi indicates that their glorification is accompanied by praise of Him.

﴿and believe in Him﴾. Its benefit, despite our knowledge that the bearers of the Throne and those around it, the angels who glorify with His praise, are believers, is to show the nobility and excellence of faith and to encourage it, just as the prophets are described in more than one place as righteous for this reason, and just as good deeds are followed by the words: ﴿Then he became of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]. Thereby he makes clear the excellence of faith. Congruence (tanasub) has been observed in His saying "and believe in Him" and "and ask forgiveness for those who believe," as if it were said: "They believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who are in a situation like theirs." In this is evidence that sharing in faith should be the strongest reason for sincere advice and compassion, even if the kinds and places are far apart.

﴿Our Lord﴾: that is, "they say: Our Lord," and this omitted element is a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿You have encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge﴾. Mercy and knowledge are what encompassed everything in meaning, since the original is: "Your mercy and Your knowledge encompassed everything," but the expression was altered from its original form by attributing the verb to the possessor of mercy and knowledge, and the two were put in the accusative as specification (tamyiz), for emphasis in describing Him with mercy and knowledge.

﴿So forgive those who repent﴾: that is, those whom You have known to repent, in keeping with the mention of mercy and knowledge.

﴿and follow Your way﴾: that is, the path of guidance to which You called.

﴿and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 8:

﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them, and those who were righteous among their fathers,﴾ "Man" (مَن) is in the accusative position, conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "them" (هُمْ) in "and admit them" (وَأدْخِلْهُمْ), or in "You have promised them" (وَعَدْتَهُمْ). The meaning is: "You have promised them, and You have promised those who were righteous among their fathers."

﴿and their spouses and their offspring. Indeed You, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾. That is: the King who cannot be overcome, and You, together with Your sovereignty and might, do not do anything devoid of wisdom, and it is required by Your wisdom that You fulfil Your promise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 9:

﴿And guard them from evil deeds﴾ That is: the requital of evil deeds, which is the punishment of the Fire,

﴿And whoever You guard from evil deeds on that Day, You have surely had mercy on him﴾ That is: the removal of the punishment,

﴿That is the great triumph.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called out to﴾ — meaning on the Day of Resurrection, when they have entered the Fire and loathe themselves. The keepers of the Fire (khazanat al-nar) will say to them: ﴿The hatred of Allah for you is greater than your hatred of yourselves﴾. That is: the hatred of Allah toward you is greater than your hatred toward yourselves. The word "you" (anfusakum) has been dropped the first time and only mentioned once, as it is understood. "Al-maqt" means the most intense hatred. The clause ﴿when you were being called to faith﴾ is governed by the first "maqt" (hatred), according to al-Zamakhshari. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to them: Allah used to loathe your commanding-to-evil selves (al-nafs al-ammara bi'l-su', the soul that orders evil), and disbelief, when the prophets were calling you to faith and you refused to accept it and chose disbelief over it, with a hatred stronger than the hatred you feel for them today while you are in the Fire, having fallen into it by following their desires. It has also been said that the meaning is: Allah's hatred of you now is greater than your hatred of one another, like His saying: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disown others and curse one another﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25]. The phrase "when you were being called" (idh tud'awna) is a reason clause (ta'lil).

The compiler of Jami' al-'Ulum (Jami' al-'Ulum) and others said: "idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb indicated by "li-maqtu Allah" (Allah's hatred). That is: Allah loathes them when they were called to faith and disbelieved. It is not governed by the first "maqt", because the phrase "li-maqtu Allah" is a subject (mubtada', the nominal subject), and it is a verbal noun (masdar), and its predicate (khabar) is "greater than your hatred of yourselves." Therefore nothing can govern "idh tud'awna," because when a verbal noun is made the subject of a predicate, nothing that belongs to its complement may be attached to it, since reporting about it indicates its completeness, while what is attached to it indicates its incompleteness. Nor is it governed by the second term (the predicate), because of the difference in the two times: they loathed themselves in the Fire, whereas they had been called to faith in the world.

﴿Then you disbelieve﴾ — that is, you persist in disbelief.

They say: ﴿Our Lord, You caused us to die twice, and You gave us life twice.﴾ That is, two deaths and two lives. By the two deaths he means: creating them as dead at first, and their dying when their appointed terms end. It is valid to call their creation a "causing to die," just as it is valid to say, "Glory be to Him who made the body of the gnat small and the body of the elephant large." There is no transfer from largeness to smallness, or from smallness to largeness. The reason is that smallness and largeness are both possible for one and the same created thing. When the Maker chooses one of the two possibilities, He has turned the created thing away from the other possibility, so turning it away from the other is treated as if it were a transfer from it.

By the two lives he means the first life and the life of resurrection (al-ba'th). This is supported by His saying: ﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die; then He will give you life again﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. It has also been said that the first death is in this world, and the second is in the grave after being brought back to life for questioning. The first life is His bringing them back to life in the grave after their death, for questioning, and the second is for resurrection.

﴿So we have confessed our sins.﴾ When they saw that causing to die and giving life had been repeated upon them, they knew that God is able to restore them, just as He is able to originate them. So they confessed their sins that they had committed, namely denying the resurrection and the acts of disobedience that followed from it.

﴿Is there any way out?﴾ From the Fire. That is, is there any kind of exit, quick or slow, by which we may be saved?

﴿Any way at all?﴾ Or is despair in fact settled beyond that, so that there is no exit and no way to it? This is the speech of one whom despair has overcome. They say this only out of bewilderment, and for this reason the answer came in accordance with it, which is His saying:

That is it, because when Allah alone was invoked you disbelieved, and when partners were associated with Him you believed. That is, that which you are in, and that there is no way out for you at all, is because of your disbelief in the Oneness of Allah and your belief in associating partners with Him.

﴿So judgment belongs to Allah﴾, Who has decreed for you the everlasting punishment,

﴿the Most High﴾, in His station, so His decree is not turned back,

﴿the Great﴾, whose dominion is mighty, so His recompense cannot be limited. It has been said: it seems the Harurites (al-Haruriyya) took their saying "There is no judgment except for Allah" from this. Qatada said: when the people of Harura (ahl Harura) came out, 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said, "Who are these?" It was said, "The Muhakkima (those who say arbitration belongs to Allah)," that is, they say, "There is no judgment except for Allah." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said, "A word of truth by which falsehood is intended."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 13:

﴿He it is who shows you His signs﴾, namely the wind, the clouds, the thunder, the lightning, the thunderbolts, and the like,

﴿and sends down for you provision from the sky﴾, and it is read with the lighter form (tukhfif, i.e. yunazzilu rather than yunazzilu with tashdid), as transmitted by Makki and Basri (the readers of Mecca and Basra),

﴿provision﴾, meaning rain, because it is the cause of sustenance (rizq),

﴿and none remembers except those who turn back (to God in repentance)﴾, meaning: none takes heed, is admonished, or draws a lesson from the signs of God except one who repents from polytheism and returns to God, for the obstinate one does not remember and is not admonished. Then he said, addressing those who turn back (al-munibin):

"So call upon Allah," meaning: worship Him,

"sincere in religion to Him," from polytheism,

"even though the disbelievers dislike it," even if that enrages your enemies, those who are not upon your religion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 40, verse 15:

﴿Exalted in degrees, Lord of the Throne, He casts the Spirit﴾: these are three predicates (akhbar) of the pronoun "He" (huwa), arranged in sequence after His words "who shows you" (alladhi yurikum). Alternatively, they are predicates of an elided subject (mubtada', "subject"). The meaning of "Exalted in degrees" is: He raises the heavens, some above others. Or: He raises the degrees of His servants in this world through rank. Or: He raises their dwellings in Paradise. "Lord of the Throne" means the Possessor of His Throne, which is above the heavens. He created it as a place for the angels to circle, to show His greatness, while being free of need within His dominion. (p-204) "The Spirit" is Jibril, peace be upon him, or the revelation by which hearts are given life.

﴿from His command﴾: that is, for the sake of His command, or by His command.

﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants, that he may warn﴾: that is, God (the subject of "casts"), or the one upon whom it is cast, who is the Prophet ﷺ. The reading of Ya'qub, "that you may warn" (liturinidh), supports this.

﴿the Day of Meeting﴾: the Day of Resurrection, because on it the people of the heavens and the people of the earth meet, as do the first and the last. "Al-talaqi" (with the final vowel as a reading variant) is read by Makki and Ya'qub.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 16:

﴿The Day they will be manifest﴾: appearing openly, with nothing concealing them, [such as] a mountain, a hill, or a building.

﴿Nothing about them will be hidden from Allah﴾, i.e., of their deeds and their states.

﴿"Whose is the dominion today?"﴾, i.e., Allah (Exalted is He) says this when no one is answering Him; then He answers Himself with His saying: ﴿"To Allah, the One, the Subduer."﴾, i.e., the One who subdued creation through death. "Today" (al-yawm) is in the accusative, governed by the meaning contained in "li-man" (whose), i.e., "For whom does dominion stand established on this day?" It was also said: a caller calls out, saying: ﴿"Whose is the dominion today?"﴾, and the people of the gathering answer him: "To Allah, the One, the Subduer."

On the Day, every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. There is no injustice today. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning. (Qur'an 40:17)

When he had established that sovereignty belongs to Allah alone on that Day, he enumerated its consequences: that every soul will be recompensed for what it earned in the world, whether good or evil; that injustice is ruled out from Him, since He is not one who wrongs His servants; and that the reckoning will not be delayed, since no account occupies Him from another account, so He reckons all creation at one time, and He is the swiftest of those who reckon.

﴿And warn them of the Day of the Imminent (al-Azifah)﴾, that is, the Resurrection. It is called that because of its *uzuf*, meaning its nearness. "The Day of the Imminent" is in apposition (*badal*) to what precedes it.

﴿When the hearts are at the throats﴾, that is, at the *taraqi* (the collarbones). It means their hearts rise from their places and cling to their throats, so they neither leave the body and die, nor return to their places and breathe and find relief.

﴿Suppressing (kazimin)﴾, holding their throats in check. The word derives from *kazama al-qirbah*, meaning he tied its mouth shut. It is a circumstantial state (*hal*) of "the hearts," understood as referring to their owners. The plural *al-kazimin* is the sound masculine plural, because the verb is attributed to them with the act of suppressing, which is an act of rational beings.

﴿For the wrongdoers﴾ (*al-zalimin*), that is, for the disbelievers.

﴿There is no close friend (hamim)﴾, one who loves them and is compassionate toward them.

﴿Nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾, that is, one who intercedes. This is a metaphor for obedience, because true obedience is only owed to one who is above you. The intended meaning is the negation of both intercession and obedience, as in the line of poetry:

"......................... and you do not see the lizard (*dabb*) creeping into it"

By this he means the negation of the lizard and of its creeping in. Although the wording could allow the negation of obedience without the negation of intercession, al-Hasan said: "By God, they will have no intercessor whatsoever."

﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾: it is a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, *maṣdar*), meaning "the treachery" (*al-khiyānah*), like *al-ʿāfiyah*, meaning "the well-being" (*al-muʿāfāh*). What is intended is the stealthy glancing at what is not lawful.

﴿And what the breasts conceal﴾: what they keep secret of trust and treachery. It was also said that it is when one looks at a non-mahram woman with desire, furtively, and then reflects in his heart on her beauty, while no one present knows of his glance or his thought. Allah knows all of that. And "He knows the treachery of the eyes" is a *khabar* (predicate) of "Huwa" (He) in His saying, "He it is who shows you His signs." It is like "He casts down the Spirit," but "He casts down the Spirit" has been given a reason by His saying: ﴿so that He may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾ [Ghafir: 15]. Then he digressed to mention the conditions of the Day of Meeting, up to His saying, "and no intercessor who is obeyed," so it became distant from its sisters for that reason.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 20:

﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾, i.e., He whose attributes are these does not judge except with justice.

﴿And those they invoke besides Him do not judge with anything﴾; their deities do not judge with anything. This is a mockery of them, because what is not described as having power is not said of it: "He judges," or "He does not judge," "you invoke," "beneficial,"

﴿Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, a confirmation of His saying: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir: 19], and a warning to them that He hears what they say, sees what they do, and will punish them for it; and an allusion to those they invoke besides Him, that they neither hear nor see.

(p-206) ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen what was the end of those who came before them?﴾ That is: the final fate of those who denied the messengers before them.

﴿They were greater than them in strength﴾. "Hum" (هم) is a separating pronoun (fasl, a pronoun that separates the subject from the predicate). Its proper place is between two definite terms. However, "أشَدَّ مِنهم" (ashadda minhum, "greater than them") resembles a definite noun in that it does not take the article "al-", so it is treated as though it were one. "Minkum" (مِنكُمْ) is a reading attributed to the Shami (the Syrian reading).

﴿And monuments in the earth﴾: that is, fortresses and palaces.

﴿So God seized them for their sins﴾: He punished them because of their sins.

﴿And they had no protector from God﴾: there was nothing that could shield them from the punishment of God.

That is: the seizing (of them) is because of the fact that,

﴿Because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved, so God seized them. Indeed He is Strong﴾, Able over everything,

﴿severe in punishment﴾, when He punishes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 23:

﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs,﴾ the nine (signs),

﴿and a manifest authority,﴾ and a clear proof.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 24:

﴿To Pharaoh and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾, "He is ﴿a sorcerer, a liar﴾." They called the manifest authority (al-sultan al-mubin) "sorcery" and "lying."

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 25:**

﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us﴾, meaning the prophethood,

﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him"﴾. That is, reinstate the killing upon them, as it was at first,

﴿and spare their women﴾, for service.

﴿But the plotting of the disbelievers is only in error﴾, meaning loss and ruin. That is, they had already carried out their killing at first, so it did not avail them. God's decree was carried out by the appearance of the one they feared, so this second killing does not avail them either. Pharaoh had stopped killing the boys, but when Musa, peace be upon him, was sent and he sensed that the matter had already come to pass, he reinstated it against them out of rage, and he thought that by this he could keep them from supporting Musa, peace be upon him. He did not know that his plotting was wasted in both instances.

(p-207) ﴿And Pharaoh said﴾ to his chiefs: ﴿"Leave me to kill Moses."﴾ Whenever he intended to kill him, they restrained him by saying: "He is not the one we fear; he is of lesser account than that, and he is only a sorcerer. If you kill him, you will place doubt in people's minds, and they will believe that you were unable to oppose him with proof." Apparently Pharaoh was certain that he was a prophet and that what he brought were signs, and that it was not sorcery; but there was deceit in him, and he was a killer and a shedder of blood over the most trivial matters. How, then, would he not kill one whom he sensed was the one who would demolish his kingdom? Rather, he feared that if he intended to kill him, he would be hastened to destruction. His saying ﴿"And let him call upon his Lord"﴾ is a true witness to the extent of his fear of him and of Moses' supplication to his Lord. His saying ﴿"Leave me to kill Moses"﴾ was a deception toward his people and a suggestion that they were the ones restraining him, whereas what restrained him was only what was in his own soul of the terror of fright.

﴿"Indeed, I fear﴾ that if I do not kill him,

﴿that he will change your religion,﴾ that he will alter what you are upon—and they used to worship him and to worship idols—

﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear﴾ — that is, Moses — ﴿in the land."﴾ The reading with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the dāl ("yuẓhira") is that of Madanī, Baṣrī and Ḥafṣ, while the others read it with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the dāl ("yaẓhara"). The first is preferable, for its agreement with "yubaddila." Corruption in the land is mutual slaughter and turmoil, by which security departs, farms and livelihoods and means of subsistence are disrupted, and people perish by killing and ruin. It is as if he said: "I fear that he will corrupt your religion for you by calling you to his religion, or that he will corrupt your worldly affairs for you by the trials that appear because of him." Those other than the people of Kufa read it as "wa-an" (and that), meaning: "I fear the corruption of your religion and your worldly life together."

﴿And Musa said﴾, when he heard what Fir'awn had done in regard to the talk of killing him among his people:

﴿Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾. In his saying "your Lord" there is an exhortation to them to follow his example, so that they seek refuge in Allah as he did and hold fast to reliance upon Him as he held fast. He said "from every arrogant one" so that his seeking refuge would include Fir'awn and others among the tyrants, and so that it would be in the manner of *ta'rid* (indirect allusion, a figure in which the intended meaning is implied rather than stated), which is more eloquent. By *takabbur* (arrogance) he meant haughtiness in refusing to submit to the truth, which is the ugliest form of arrogance and the clearest indicator of the baseness of its bearer and of the extreme (p-208) extent of his injustice. He said ﴿who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾ because when arrogance, denial of recompense, and indifference to the outcome come together in a man, he has gathered the causes of harshness and audacity against Allah and His servants, and he leaves no grave sin without committing it.

"*ʿudtu*" (عُذْتُ) and "*ludtu*" (لُذْتُ) are two related forms (both meaning "I sought refuge"). "*ʿuttu*" (عُتُّ), with idgham (assimilation of the two identical consonants), is read by Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and ʿAli.

﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said﴾. It is said that he was a Copt, a cousin of Pharaoh, who had secretly believed in Musa. "مِنَ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ" (min āli Fir'awn, "from the family of Pharaoh") is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "رَجُلٌ" (rajul, "man"). It is also said that he was an Israelite, and in that case "مِن آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ" is a complement (ṣilah) of "يَكْتُمُ" (yaktumu, "conceals"), meaning he concealed his faith from the family of Pharaoh. His name was Sam'an, or Habib, or Kharbil, or Hizbil. The apparent view is the first.

﴿Do you kill a man because he says﴾, "لِأنْ يَقُولَ" (li-an yaqūla, "because he says"). This is a great denunciation from him, as if he had said: Do you commit this abominable act, which is the killing of a forbidden soul, when your only reason for committing it is a word of truth, namely his saying: ﴿My Lord is Allah﴾? He is your Lord too, not only his Lord.

﴿And he has certainly come to you﴾. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿with clear proofs from your Lord﴾. This means that he did not come to confirm his statement with a single proof, but with proofs from the One to whom lordship is attributed. This is a method of leading them step by step (istidrāj) toward acknowledging Him.

﴿And if he is a liar, his lie will be upon him; and if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾. He argued against them by way of division (taqsīm), for he is either a liar or a truthful man. If he is a liar, the burden of his lie falls upon him and does not pass beyond him. If he is truthful, some of the punishment he promises you will strike you. He did not say "all of what he promises you," although it is a promise from a prophet who speaks the truth. This was out of consideration for them (mudārāh) and in keeping with the path of fairness, so he used the wording that was closer to their acceptance of it. There is no negation in it of the befalling of all of it. It is as if he had said to them: perhaps what, in his truthfulness, will befall you is some of what he promises you, namely the hastened punishment, and in that is your destruction. He had promised them the punishment of this world and of the Hereafter. Placing the liar before the truthful in this way is also of this kind. Interpreting "some" as "all" is spurious (muzayyaf).

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor﴾, meaning one who exceeds the limit.

﴿a liar﴾, in his claim. This also belongs to the category of courtesy (mujāmalah). The meaning is that if he is a transgressor and a liar, Allah will forsake him and destroy him, and so you will be rid of him. Or, if he were a transgressor and a liar, Allah would not have guided him with prophethood, nor would He have strengthened him with clear proofs. It is also said that he gave the impression that he meant by "the transgressor" Musa, whereas he meant by it Pharaoh. (p-209)

O my people, the dominion is yours today, *ẓāhirīna* (dominant), *ʿāliyīna* (exalted). It is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of *kum* in *lakum*.

﴿on the earth﴾, in the land of Egypt.

﴿So who will help us against the might of God if it comes upon us?﴾ He means: the kingdom of Egypt is yours, and you have risen above the people and subdued them. So do not ruin your affair for yourselves, and do not expose yourselves to the might of God, that is, His punishment. For you have no power against it if it comes to you, and no one can shield you from it. He said "will help us" and "came upon us" because he was one of them by kinship, and to inform them that the counsel he gives them is something in which he shares with them.

﴿Pharaoh said, "I show you only what I see."﴾ That is: I do not advise you with any opinion except what I see of killing him. That is, I approve of nothing but killing him, and what you are saying is not right.

﴿And I guide you only to the path of right conduct,﴾ to the path of correctness and righteousness. I inform you only of what I know to be correct, and I withhold nothing of it, nor do I conceal from you anything contrary to what I make known. That is, his tongue and his heart agree on what he says, yet he was lying. He was sensing a severe fear from the side of Moses, peace be upon him, but he was steeling himself. Had he not sensed it, he would not have consulted anyone, and the matter would not have stopped at a mere hint.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 30:

﴿And the one who had believed said, "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions."﴾ I.e., like their days, because when he attributed it to "the factions" and explained them with His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 31:

﴿Like the custom of the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, and those after them﴾. And it is not confused that each faction among them had a day of destruction; he limited it to the singular of the plural. The custom (da'b) of these people is their persistence (du'ub) in their deeds, from disbelief, denial, and all the other sins, and that being constant and continuous on their part, never slackening from it. There must be an elision of a genitive (mudaf), meaning: "like the recompense of their custom." The accusative of the second "mithl" (ﻣِﺜْﻞَ) is because it is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to the first "mithl."

﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾. That is: Allah does not desire to wrong His servants, so that He would punish them without a sin, or exceed the measure of punishment they deserve. The meaning is that their destruction was justice, because they deserved it by their deeds. This is more eloquent than His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], since He made the negated thing the desire of an indefinite injustice (ẓulm munakkar). Whoever is far from desiring any injustice toward his servants is even further and further from injustice. The interpretation of the Mu'tazilah, that He does not desire for them that they wrong (one another), is far-fetched, because the people of the language said: when a man says to another, "I do not desire injustice against you," its meaning is "I do not desire to wrong you." This is a warning of the punishment of this world. Then He warned them of the punishment of the Hereafter with His saying:

"And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling out" — that is, the Day of Resurrection. "At-Tanad" is read by Makki and Ya'qub in both states (of pausing and continuing), and retaining the ya' (ي) is the original form, while omitting it is acceptable, because the kasra indicates the ya', and the ending of these verses rests on the dal (د). This is like what God (Exalted) recounts in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], ﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out﴾ [al-A'raf: 48]. It is also said: a caller will call out, "Verily, so-and-so has attained a happiness after which he will never be wretched, and verily, so-and-so has suffered a wretchedness after which he will never be happy."

On the Day you will turn back in flight, withdrawing from the place of reckoning toward the Fire,

﴿You will have no protector from God﴾, that is, from the punishment of God,

﴿no preserver﴾, one who prevents, and repels. ﴿And whomever God leads astray, for him there is no guide﴾, one who gives guidance.

﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs﴾: he was Joseph son of Jacob, peace be upon them both. It is also said: Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub. He was a prophet among them for twenty years. It is also said that the Pharaoh of Moses was the Pharaoh of Joseph, who lived long enough to reach his time. It is also said that he was another Pharaoh. He rebuked them, saying that Joseph had come to them before Moses with miracles.

﴿So you continued in doubt about what he brought you﴾: you were skeptical of it, and you did not cease to be doubters.

﴿Until, when he died, you said: "Allah will never send after him a messenger"﴾: a judgment from your own selves, without evidence. That is, you persisted in your disbelief and assumed that He would not renew the establishing of proof against you.

﴿Thus Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor, a doubter﴾: that is, in the manner of this misguidance, Allah leaves astray every transgressor in his disobedience, every doubter who is uncertain about his religion.

﴿الَّذِينَ يُجادِلُونَ﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for "man huwa musrif" (﴿مَن هو مُسْرِفٌ﴾). It is permissible to substitute it for that phrase, even though it is plural, because the intended referent is not one single transgressor but every transgressor.

﴿فِي آياتِ اللهِ﴾: in repelling them and in invalidating them.

﴿بِغَيْرِ سُلْطانٍ﴾: without authority, meaning without proof.

﴿أتاهم كَبُرَ مَقْتًا﴾: that is, it became great in hatred. The subject of "kabura" is the pronoun referring to "man huwa musrif". That pronoun is plural in meaning (*jam' ma'nan*) but singular in form (*muwahhad lafzan*). So the *badal* is construed according to its meaning, while the pronoun referring back to it is construed according to its wording.

It is also permissible to read "alladhina" as nominative, as an inchoative subject (*mubtada'*). On this reading, it is necessary to supply an elided noun (*mudaf* that is omitted) to which the pronoun in "kabura" refers. Its estimated form is: "jidal alladhina yujadiluna kabura maqtan" (the disputing of those who dispute has become great in hatred).

﴿عِنْدَ اللهِ وعِنْدَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كَذَلِكَ يَطْبَعُ اللهُ عَلى كُلِّ قَلْبِ مُتَكَبِّرٍ جَبّارٍ﴾: thus Allah seals every heart of an arrogant, tyrannical person, in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believe.

"Qalbin" is read with tanwin by Abu 'Amr. The heart is described as arrogant and tyrannical because it is the source of these two qualities, just as you say, "the ear heard." This is like His saying, ﴿فَإنَّهُ آثِمٌ قَلْبُهُ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:283: "then indeed his heart is sinful"), although the one who is sinful is actually the whole person.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 36:

﴿And Pharaoh said﴾, to deceive his people, or out of his own ignorance,

﴿O Haman, build for me a tower﴾, that is: a palace. It is also said: al-sarh (lofty structure) is a building that is conspicuous and not hidden from the observer, even if he is far away. From it comes the expression "al-shay' sarah (the thing became clear)", meaning it became manifest.

﴿la'alli﴾, and with the ya' pronounced with a fatha (la'alliya), is the reading of the Hijazi (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), the Syrian (Ibn 'Amir) and Abu 'Amr,

﴿ablughu al-asbab﴾, then he (the phrase) was put in apposition to it (la'alli), to magnify its importance and to make clear that he intends a momentous matter.

(p. 212) ﴿asbāba as-samāwāt﴾ means their paths, their gateways, and whatever leads to them. Anything that brings you to something is a *sabab* (means) to it, such as a rope (*rishā'*) and the like.

﴿fa-aṭṭali'a﴾ is read with the accusative (*naṣb*) by Ḥafṣ, as a response to the optative (*tarajjī*), likening the expression of hope (*tarajjī*) to the expression of wish (*tamannī*). Others read it in the nominative (*raf'*), as a conjunction (*'aṭf*) on *abluġu* (I may reach).

﴿ilā ilāhi Mūsā﴾: the meaning is "so that I may look at him."

﴿wa-innī la-aẓunnuhu﴾, that is, Mūsā, ﴿kādhiban﴾ in his saying, "He has a god other than me."

﴿wa-kadhālika﴾: likewise, like that adornment and that turning away.

﴿zuyyina li-Fir'awna sū'u 'amalihi wa-ṣuddda 'ani as-sabīl﴾: "The evil of his deeds was made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the [straight] path." The reading with the *ṣād* vowelled with a fatḥa (*ṣuddda* → *wa-ṣaddda*), by all readers other than the Kufans and Yaʿqūb, means "he caused others to be barred" (*ṣadḍan*), or "he himself turned away" (*ṣudūdan*). The one who adorns is Satan, through his whispering, as in His saying: ﴿And Satan made their deeds attractive to them and barred them from the way﴾ [al-Naml: 24]. Or it is God (exalted is He), and similar to it is: ﴿We made their deeds attractive to them, so they wander blindly﴾ [al-Naml: 4].

﴿wa-mā kaydu Fir'awna illā fī tabāb﴾: the scheming of Pharaoh is nothing but ruin, that is, loss and destruction.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 38:

﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct."﴾ "Ittabi'uni" (follow me) is read in both states (pausal and continuous) by Makki, Ya'qub and Sahl.

﴿أهْدِكم سَبِيلَ الرَشادِ﴾ — "al-rashad" is the opposite of "al-ghayy" (misguidance, error). In it there is an implicit allusion (ta'rid), close to an explicit statement (tasrih), that what Pharaoh and his people follow is the path of misguidance. He first stated the matter in summary (ijmal), then explained it in detail, beginning with a condemnation of the worldly life (dunya) and a belittling of its worth, in his words:

O my people, this worldly life is only a fleeting enjoyment (matā‘) — a brief pleasure. So inclining toward it (al-ikhlād ilayhā) is the root of evil and the source of trials. He followed this with the magnification of the Hereafter, and made clear that it is the true homeland and the abode of permanence, by His saying: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter is the abode of settlement.﴾ Then he mentioned deeds, both their evil and their good, and the outcome of each of them, so that he would deter from what destroys and encourage toward what brings one near, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 40, verse 40:

﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without reckoning.﴾ "*Yudkhalūna*" (they are made to enter; passive form), read by Makki, Basri, Yazid and Abu Bakr. (p-213) Then he weighed the two calls against each other: his call to the religion of God, whose fruit is salvation, and their call to taking *andād* (rivals to God), whose end is the Fire, by his saying:

And O my people, what is (the matter) with me? I call you to salvation, while you call me to the Fire.

Note on the reading: the yā' in ﴿مَا لِي﴾ is pronounced with a fatḥah (لِيَ), a reading transmitted from the Ḥijāzī (Meccan) reciters and Abū ʿAmr.

Here the "salvation" (al-najāh) means Paradise.

﴿وَتَدْعُونَنِي إِلَى النَّارِ﴾ — "and you call me to the Fire."

﴿You invite me to disbelieve in Allah﴾: this is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) of the first ﴿you invite me﴾. It is said: "*da'ahu ila kadha*" (he invited him to such-and-such) and "*da'ahu lahu*" (he invited him to it), just as it is said: "*hadahu ila al-tariq*" (he guided him to the way) and "*hadahu lahu*" (he guided him to it).

﴿and I associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge﴾, meaning regarding His *rububiyyah* (lordship). The intended meaning of negating knowledge is negating the known object, as if he said: "and I associate with Him that which is not a god, and how can that which is not a god be known as a god?!"

﴿And I invite you to the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾, who is Allah, glory be to Him and exalted. The repetition of the call is to increase their alertness and to awaken them from the drowsiness of heedlessness. It also indicates that they are his people, and that he is from the family of Pharaoh. The *waw* (and) was used in the third call but not in the second, because the second follows a statement that is an explanation of the general matter and an elaboration of it, unlike the third.

According to the grammarians of Basra (al-Basriyyun), ﴿Lā jarama﴾ ("Without doubt"): "lā" is a rejection of what his people had called him to, and "jarama" is a verb meaning "haqqa" (it is established/true). "Anna," together with what follows it in its clause, is its subject, meaning: "It is established and necessary that the invalidity of their call is true."

﴿Anna mā tad'ūnanī ilayhi laysa lahu da'watun fī al-dunyā wa-lā fī al-ākhirah﴾ ("That which you call me to has no call, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter"). Its meaning: that which you call me to has never had a call to itself. That is, it is the right of the God worthy of worship to call His servants to obey Him, whereas what you call to, and to worship it, does not call to that, nor does it claim lordship. Or its meaning: it has no answering of a call in this world or the Hereafter. Or it means a call that is answered: the call that has no answer and no benefit is treated like "lā da'wata" (no call). Or the answer is named by the name of the call, just as the act that is recompensed is named "al-jazā'" (the recompense), in his saying: "As you judge, so you will be judged" (kamā tadīnu tudān).

﴿Wa-anna maraddanā ilā Allāh﴾ ("and that our return is to God"), that our return is to Him.

﴿Wa-anna al-musrifīna﴾ ("and that the transgressors"), that the polytheists.

﴿Hum aṣḥāb al-nār﴾ ("they are the companions of the Fire").

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 44:

﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾, i.e., of the counsel, when the punishment descends,

﴿And I entrust﴾, and I submit, ﴿my affair﴾, and with the ya' vowelled with a fatha, "Madani and Abu 'Amr,"

﴿to Allah﴾, because they had threatened him,

﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾, of their deeds and their final destinations.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 45:

﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾: the severity of their scheming, and what they intended of inflicting various kinds of punishment upon whoever opposed them. It is said that he (the believer) went out from among them, fleeing to a mountain, so they sent nearly a thousand men in pursuit of him. Some of them were eaten by wild beasts, and whoever returned from them, Pharaoh crucified.

﴿And there befell﴾, that is, came down upon, ﴿the folk of Pharaoh the evil of the punishment﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 46:

﴿The Fire﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "the evil of the punishment," or the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), as if it were said: "What is the evil of the punishment?" And it was said: "It is the Fire." Or it is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is: ﴿They are exposed to it﴾. Their being exposed to it (ʿarḍuhum ʿalayhā) means their being burned by it. It is said: "The imam exposed the captives to the sword ('araḍa al-imām al-usārā ʿalā al-sayf)," when he killed them with it.

﴿Morning and evening﴾ means: at these two times they are tormented with the Fire. As for what lies between them, they may either be tormented with another kind (of punishment), or relief may be given to them. It is also permissible that "morning and evening" is an expression for continuity (al-dawām). This is in the world.

﴿And on the day the Hour arises﴾, it will be said to the guardians of Hell (khazanat Jahannam): ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh﴾. From "al-idkhal" (causing to enter). Madani, Hamza, ʿAli, Ḥafs, Khalaf and Yaʿqub read it this way; others read "udkhulū" (enter), meaning: it will be said to them, "Enter, O people of Pharaoh," ﴿to the severest punishment﴾, i.e., the punishment of Hell. And this verse is evidence for the punishment of the grave (ʿadhāb al-qabr).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 47:

﴿And when they dispute⁠﴾, i.e., remember the time of their quarrelling,

﴿in the Fire, and the weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾, meaning the leaders,

﴿"Indeed we were your followers"⁠﴾, i.e., tabi'un (followers, pl. of tabi'), like khadam (servants), the plural of khadim (servant),

﴿"So will you relieve us of a portion"⁠﴾, i.e., dafi'un (repellers), 

﴿"of the Fire"⁠﴾, i.e., juz' (a part).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 48:

﴿Those who were arrogant will say: "Indeed, we are all in it."﴾ The tanwin (nunation) here is a substitute (ʿiwad) for the genitive noun that has been omitted, meaning: "Indeed, all of us are in it; no one can avail anyone else."

﴿Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants.﴾ He has decided between them by admitting the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 49:

﴿And those who are in the Fire say to the guardians of Hell﴾, that is, to those entrusted with punishing its inhabitants. And why did he not say "to its guardians" (likhazanatiha)? Because mentioning Jahannam (Hell) carries awe and dread. It is also possible that Jahannam is the deepest part of the Fire, from the saying "bi'run jahannam" (a well whose bottom is far away), since it is deep at the bottom, and in it are the most obstinate and most rebellious of the disbelievers. So perhaps the angels appointed to punish those people are more responsive to supplication, due to their greater nearness to Allah (Exalted), and therefore the inhabitants of the Fire deliberately seek supplication from them,

﴿Call upon your Lord, that He may lighten for us a day﴾, by the measure of a day of the worldly life,

﴿of the punishment﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 50:

﴿They said﴾, that is: the guardians (al-khazana), rebuking them, after a long period [of time].

﴿Did there not come to you﴾, that is: was the matter not so, that ﴿your messengers came to you﴾ — and His saying ﴿your messengers came to you﴾ is an explanation of the matter —

﴿with clear proofs﴾, with miracles.

﴿They said﴾, that is: the disbelievers.

﴿Yes, they said﴾, that is: the guardians, mocking them.

﴿Then call [upon Him]﴾, you yourselves, and there is no answering of your supplication.

﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, that is, in falsehood. This is from the words of Allah (exalted be He), and it is possible that it is from the words of the guardians.

Indeed, We surely help Our messengers and those who believe, in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses will stand. That is, in this world and in the Hereafter. It means that He overcomes them in both abodes together, through the proof and through victory over their opponents, even if after some time.

"Yawm" (day) is in the accusative (naṣb), treated as being in the place of the prepositional phrase (jār wa majrūr), as when you say: "I came to you in yesterday and today."

"Al-ashhād" is the plural of "shāhid" (witness), like "ṣāḥib" (companion) and "aṣḥāb" (companions). It refers to the prophets and the guardians (al-ḥafaẓa). The prophets bear witness before the Lord of Might against the disbelievers for their denial, and the guardians bear witness against the children of Adam for the deeds they did.

"Taqūmu" (stand). Al-Razi, from Hisham.

"On the Day when their excuses will not benefit the wrongdoers" — this is a substitution (badal) for "the Day when there arises" [i.e., the day when the witnesses stand up], meaning: their excuse will not be accepted. "Yanfa'u" (benefit) — read by al-Kufi (Hafs? no, here "al-Kufi" refers to the Kufan reader) and Nafi'.

﴿And for them is the curse﴾: distance from the mercy of Allah.

﴿And for them is the evil abode﴾: that is, the evil of the abode of the Hereafter, which is its punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 53:

﴿And We certainly gave Musa (Moses) the guidance﴾. He means by it everything that he brought in matters of the religion: of the miracles (mu'jizat), the Torah, and the laws (shara'i'),

﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book﴾, that is: the Torah, the Gospel (Injil), and the Psalms (Zabur), because "al-Kitab" (the Book) is a genus (jins).

Guidance and a reminder (hudan wa-dhikra): guidance (irshadan) and admonition (tadhkira). Their being in the accusative is either as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) or as a circumstantial state (hal).

For those of understanding (li-uli al-albab): for those possessed of intellects (li-dhawi al-'uqul).

﴿So be patient﴾ over what your people make you swallow of grief,

﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾, meaning: "Indeed, what My promise has preceded regarding your victory and the elevation of your word is true,"

﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾, i.e., for the sin of your community,

﴿So be patient, indeed the promise of Allah is true, and ask forgiveness for your sin, and glorify the praise of your Lord in the evening and the morning﴾, i.e., persist in worshipping your Lord and in praising Him. It was said: they are the two prayers of ʿAṣr (the afternoon prayer) and Fajr (the dawn prayer). It was also said: say, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him."

(p. 217) There is no pause (waqf) on this, because the predicate (khabar) of "inna" (indeed, a grammatical particle used for emphasis) is: ﴿there is in their breasts nothing but pride﴾, meaning arrogance (ta'azzum), which is the desire for precedence and leadership, and that no one should be above them. Therefore they opposed you and rejected Your verses, out of fear that you would surpass them and they would be under your authority, your command and your prohibition, for prophethood brings beneath it every kingship and leadership. Or it is the desire that prophethood would belong to them rather than to you, out of envy and insolence, and this is indicated by their saying: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11]. Or it is the desire to repel the verses through disputation.

﴿They will not attain it﴾: they will not attain what pride requires and entails, which is the object of their desire, whether that is leadership, prophethood, or the repelling of the verses.

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾: take refuge in Him from the plotting of one who envies you and transgresses against you.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾: of what you say and what they say,

﴿the All-Seeing﴾: of what you do and what they do. So He is your helper against them and your protector from their evil.

The Creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind. Since their disputing concerning the signs of Allah involved denying the Resurrection, which is the root of the dispute and its axis, they were argued with the creation of the heavens and the earth, because they acknowledged that Allah is their Creator. For whoever is able to create them, despite their greatness, is more able to create man, despite his lowliness.

﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾, because they do not reflect, due to the dominance of heedlessness over them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 58:

﴿Nor are the blind and the seeing alike, nor those who believe and do righteous deeds, nor the evildoer﴾. "Lā" (لا) is superfluous (zā'idah),

﴿little do you remember﴾: tatta'izūn (تتعظون), "you take heed". It is read with two tā's (بِتاءَيْنِ) by "Kūfī" (كُوفِيٌّ, the reader of Kufa), and with a yā' and a tā' (وبِياءٍ وتاءٍ) by "others" (غَيْرُهُمْ). "Qalīlan" (قَلِيلًا) is an adjective (ṣifah) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar maḥdhūf), meaning: "you remember with little remembrance" (تَذَكُّرًا قَلِيلًا تَتَذَكَّرُونَ). "Mā" (ما) is a superfluous particle (ṣilah zā'idah).

﴿Indeed, the Hour is surely coming; there is no doubt about it﴾. It must come, and it is not doubted that it will come, because there must be a recompense, lest the creation of creatures be only for annihilation.

﴿But most people do not believe﴾, they do not give credence to it.

﴿وَقالَ رَبُّكُمُ ادْعُونِي﴾ "And your Lord said: Call upon Me" ('uduni, "worship Me"),

﴿أسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ﴾ ("I will answer you"): ("uthibukum," "I will reward you"). Thus, *du'a'* (supplication) in the sense of *'ibadah* (worship) is frequent in the Qur'an, and the proof for this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disdain My worship﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Supplication is worship," and he (ﷺ) recited this verse. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Affirm My oneness and I will forgive you." This is an explanation of supplication as worship, and then of worship as *tawhid* (affirmation of Allah's oneness). It was also said: "Ask Me and I will give you."

﴿سَيَدْخُلُونَ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("they will enter Hell"). Read as "*sa-yudkhalūna*" (they will be made to enter), by Makki and Abu 'Amr.

﴿داخِرِينَ﴾ ("humiliated"): *ṣāghirīn*, meaning abased.

﴿It is Allah who made for you the night that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight﴾. This is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), meaning *mubsiran* ("giving sight") in the sense of *mubsaran fihi* ("seen by means of it"), because seeing in reality belongs to the people of the day. He joined *al-layl* ("the night") with the object of purpose (al-maf'ul lahu) and *al-nahar* ("the day") with the circumstantial accusative (al-hal), though neither was a circumstantial accusative or an object of purpose for the other, out of regard for the rule of correspondence (ri'ayat haqq al-muqabala, "balance of opposites"), since the two are opposites in meaning, each performing the function of the other. Also, if it were said *li-tubsiru fihi* ("that you may see by it"), the eloquence found in the metaphorical attribution would be lost. And if it were said *sakinan* ("still"), the literal would not be distinguished from the figurative, since the night is described as still in its literal sense. Do you not see the saying of the Arabs: "A still night (*layl saj*), and calm (*sakin*), without wind"?

﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾. He did not say *lamufdil* ("a bestower") or *lamutafaddil* ("one who bestows graciously"), because the purpose is to make *fadl* ("bounty") indefinite, so that it becomes a bounty that nothing else can match, and this is only achieved through the use of the indefinite form.

﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾. He did not say *wa-lakinna aktharahum* ("but most of them"), so that the mention of "mankind" would not be repeated, because in this repetition there is a specification of ingratitude for the blessing upon them, and that it is they who reject the bounty of Allah and do not give thanks for it, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful﴾ [al-Hajj: 66], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is a great wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 62:

﴿Such is﴾ Allah, who created for you the night and the day,

﴿Allah, your Lord, the Creator of everything; there is no god but He﴾: these are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifa), meaning that He is the one who combines these attributes: lordship (rububiyya), divinity (ilahiyya), the creation of everything, and oneness (wahdaniyya).

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ That is: how, and from what direction, are you diverted from worshipping Him to worshipping idols?!

Thus are those turned away who used to deny the signs of God. (40:63)

That is: everyone who denies the signs of God, without reflecting upon them and without seeking the truth, is turned away just as they were turned away.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 64:

﴿Allah is the One who made the earth a place of settlement for you﴾, i.e., a resting place (mustaqarran),

﴿and the sky a building﴾, i.e., a ceiling above you,

﴿and fashioned you and perfected your forms﴾. It has been said: He did not create any living creature with a more beautiful form than the human being. And it has been said: He did not create you upside down like the beasts,

﴿and provided you with good things﴾, i.e., delicious things (al-ladhidhat),

﴿That is Allah, your Lord. So blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 65:

﴿He is the Living; there is no god but Him, so call upon Him,﴾ so worship Him,

﴿sincere in obedience to Him, devoting religion (al-din) to Him﴾, i.e., the obedience, free from shirk (associating partners with Allah) and riya' (showing off), saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "Whoever says: 'There is no god but Allah,' let him then say immediately after it: 'All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 66:

When the disbelievers asked him (ﷺ) to worship idols, this was revealed: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides God, now that the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord.﴾ The "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) are the Qur'an. It is also said they are reason (al-'aql) and revelation (al-wahy).

﴿And I have been commanded to submit (aslima)﴾: to be upright (astaqim) and to yield (anqad).

﴿to the Lord of the worlds.﴾

(p-220) ﴿He it is who created you﴾, i.e., your origin (aslakum),

﴿from dust, then from a drop [of semen], then from a clinging clot, then He brings you forth as a child﴾. He mentioned the singular because the purpose is to explain the species (jins).

﴿Then [He lets you live] that you may reach your full strength (ashuddakum)﴾: this is connected to an omitted element, its implied sense being, "then He keeps you alive so that you may reach..." Likewise ﴿then that you may become elders (shuyukhan)﴾, read with a kasra on the shin by Makki, Hamzah, Ali, Hammad, Yahya and al-A'sha.

﴿And among you is he who is taken in death before [that]﴾, i.e., before reaching full strength, or before old age,

﴿and that you may reach an appointed term (ajalan musamman)﴾. Its meaning: and He does that so that you may reach an appointed term, which is the time of death, or the Day of Resurrection,

﴿so that perhaps you will use your reason (ta'qilun)﴾: [reflecting on] the lessons (ibar) and proofs (hujaj) that are in this.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 68:

﴿He is the One who gives life and causes death. So when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ That is: it comes into being swiftly, without any difficulty or effort.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 69:

﴿Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah? How are they turned away?﴾ The dispute (al-jidal) is mentioned in this surah in three places, so it is permissible that it refers to three groups, or three categories, or that it is for emphasis.

ﷻ

"Those who deny the Book", meaning the Qur'an,

"and that with which We sent Our messengers", meaning from the scriptures,

"then they will come to know."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 71:

﴿When the shackles are around their necks﴾. "Idh" (إذْ) is an adverb of past time, and what is meant by it here is the future, like His saying: ﴿But they will come to know﴾. This is because future matters, when they are in the reports of God (Exalted), are certain, so He expressed them with the wording of what has already been and has occurred, while the meaning is future.

﴿And the chains﴾: a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "al-aghlal" (الأغلال, the shackles), and the predicate is "fi aʿnaqihim" (فِي أعْناقِهِمْ, around their necks). The meaning is: "When the shackles and the chains are around their necks,"

﴿they are dragged﴾

Verse 72 of Surah Ghafir (40): "In the boiling water, then in the Fire they are burned."

"In the boiling water" (fi al-hamim): they are dragged (yujarruna) through hot water.

"Then in the Fire they are kindled" (thumma fi al-nari yuskhararun): from "sajara al-tannur" (he filled the oven with fuel), meaning that they are filled with the Fire, which surrounds them, and they are kindled with fire, their insides filled with it.

Surah 40 (Ghafir), verse 73, with al-Nasafi's commentary (Madarik al-Tanzil):

﴿Then it will be said to them﴾, that is: the guardians (al-Khazanah) will say to them,

﴿"Where are those you used to associate [with God]?"﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 74:

﴿مِن دُونِ اللهِ﴾ ("Besides Allah"): meaning the idols that you used to worship.

﴿قالُوا ضَلُّوا عَنّا﴾ ("They will say: They have strayed from us"): they have vanished from our sight, so we do not see them and do not benefit from them.

﴿بَلْ لَمْ نَكُنْ نَدْعُو مِن قَبْلُ شَيْئًا﴾ ("Nay, we used not to call upon anything before"): that is, it has become clear to us that they were nothing, and by worshipping them we were worshipping nothing, just as you say: "I thought that so-and-so was something, but when I tested him, he was not anything," when you have experienced him and found no good in him.

﴿كَذَلِكَ يُضِلُّ اللهُ الكافِرِينَ﴾ ("Thus does Allah lead the disbelievers astray"): like the straying of their gods from them, He makes them stray from their gods, so that even if they seek the gods, or the gods seek them, they will not meet. Or, just as He led these disputants astray, He leads all the other disbelievers astray, those of whom it is known that they chose misguidance over the religion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 75:

﴿That﴾, the punishment that has come upon you,

﴿because you used to exult in the land without right, and because you used to behave insolently﴾. This refers to the exultation (al-farah) and insolence (al-maraḥ) you had, without right, which is shirk (associating partners with God) and the worship of idols. Then it will be said to them:

﴿Enter the gates of Hell,﴾ the seven, which are apportioned to you. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a portion apportioned [to them]﴾ [al-Hijr: 44]. ﴿Abiding therein﴾, meaning: destined to abide eternally,

﴿Wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾, those who are arrogant toward the truth. It is Hell.

﴿Fa-iṣbir﴾ (So be patient), O Muhammad,

﴿inna waʿda Allāh﴾ (indeed the promise of God), concerning the destruction of the disbelievers,

﴿ḥaqq﴾ (is true), meaning: existing.

﴿Fa-immā nurayannaka﴾ (So whether We show you). Its original form is "fa-in nurika" (fa-in nurika), and "mā" (mā) is an added particle to emphasize the meaning of the conditional. For this reason the nūn of emphasis (nūn al-tawkīd) was attached to the verb. Do you not see that you would not say "in tukrimanī ukrimka" (in tukrimanī ukrimka, "if you honor me, I will honor you"), but rather "immā tukrimanī ukrimka" (immā tukrimanī ukrimka, "whether you honor me, I will honor you")?

﴿baʿḍa alladhī naʿiduhum aw natawaffayannaka fa-ilaynā yurjaʿūn﴾ (some of what We promise them, or We cause you to die, then to Us they will be returned). This conditional clause is connected to "natawaffayannaka" (natawaffayannaka, "We cause you to die"), and the answer (jawāb) of "nurayannaka" (nurayannaka, "We show you") is omitted. Its implied meaning is: "And whether We show you some of the punishment We promise them, namely being killed on the day of Badr, then that is it; or if We cause you to die before the day of Badr, then to Us they will be returned on the Day of Resurrection, and We will take revenge on them with the most severe vengeance."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 78:

﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you﴾, to their peoples,

﴿Of them are those We have related to you, and of them are those We have not related to you﴾. It is said: Allah sent eight thousand prophets, four thousand from the Children of Israel and four thousand from the rest of mankind. And from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed Allah (Exalted) sent a black prophet, and he is among those whose story is not mentioned in the Qur'an."

﴿And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah﴾. This is the answer to their demanding signs out of obstinacy. That is to say: We have sent many messengers, and it was not for any one of them to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah. So how could I bring a sign of what you propose? Unless Allah wills and permits its coming.

﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾, i.e., the Day of Resurrection. This is a threat and a rejection following their demand for signs.

﴿The matter will be decided with truth, and the falsifiers will lose therein﴾, the obstinate ones who demanded signs out of obstinacy.

God Who made for you the cattle (khalaqa, "created"), namely the camels,

so that you may ride some of them and eat some of them. That is: so that you may ride some of them and eat some of them.

(p-223) ﴿And He shows you His signs; so which of Allah's signs will you deny?﴾ — that they are from Allah. "Ayya" (which) is in the accusative, governed by "tunkirun" (you deny). It has come in the widespread dialect, whereas your saying "fa-ayyata āyāti Allāh" is rare, because distinguishing the masculine from the feminine in nouns that are not adjectives, such as "ḥimār" (donkey) and "ḥimāra" (she-donkey), is strange, and it is even stranger in the case of "ayyu," because of its vagueness.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 82:

﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them,﴾ in number,

﴿and greater in strength,﴾ in body,

﴿and in monuments in the land,﴾ palaces and fortresses (maṣāniʿ),

﴿then what they used to earn did not avail them.﴾ "Mā" is negative (nāfiyah).

﴿When their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in the knowledge they had﴾. He means their knowledge of worldly affairs and their understanding of managing them, as He says: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Rum: 7]. When the messengers came to them with the sciences of the religions, which are the furthest thing from their knowledge because they urge the renunciation of this world, the restraint from its pleasures and desires, they did not give them any attention. They belittled them, mocked them, and believed that there is no knowledge more beneficial or more productive of gains than their own. So they rejoiced in it. Or the reference is to the knowledge of the philosophers (falasifa) and the materialists (dahriyyun, those who deny a Creator and attribute events to time). Whenever they heard of the revelation of God, they rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets in comparison with their own. It is related of Socrates (Suqrat) that he heard of Moses (peace be upon him), and it was said to him: "If only you would emigrate to him." He replied: "We are a refined people, so we have no need of someone to refine us." Or the meaning is: they rejoiced at the knowledge that the messengers had, a rejoicing of laughter and mockery at it, as if He said: "They mocked the clear proofs and what they brought of the knowledge of revelation, exulting and boastful." This is supported by His saying: ﴿And what they used to mock at encompassed them﴾. Or the rejoicing belongs to the messengers, meaning: when the messengers saw their ignorance (p-224) and their mockery of the truth, and knew the evil end awaiting them and the punishment that would befall them for their ignorance and mockery, they rejoiced in the knowledge they had been given and thanked God for it, and ﴿the consequence of their ignorance and mockery encompassed the disbelievers﴾.

﷽

﴿Then when they saw Our might⁠—﴾ that is, the severity of Our punishment,

﴿they said, "We believe in God alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him."﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 40, verse 85:

﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment.﴾ That is: it was not valid, and it was not fitting that their faith should benefit them. ﴿The Sunnah of Allah﴾ — it stands in the position of ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ and similar infinitive forms used for emphasis —

﴿which has already passed among His servants﴾: that faith does not benefit at the time the punishment descends, and that the punishment descends upon those who deny the messengers.

﴿And the disbelievers were lost there﴾. "There" (hunalika) is a place, used figuratively for a time. The disbelievers are lost at every moment, but their loss becomes evident when they witness the punishment. The purpose of the repetition of the particles "fa" (then/so) in these verses is that "fa-ma aghnā ʿanhum" (so what they had gained did not avail them) is the result of His saying "they were more numerous than them," and "fa-lammā jāʾat-hum rusuluhum" (so when their messengers came to them) serves as an explanation and elaboration of His saying "fa-ma aghnā ʿanhum," like your saying: "Zayd was given wealth, so he withheld what is good, so he did not do kindness to the poor." And "fa-lammā raʾaw baʾsanā" (so when they saw Our punishment) follows His saying "fa-lammā jāʾat-hum," as if He had said: "They disbelieved, then when they saw Our punishment they believed." Likewise "fa-lam yaku yanfaʿu-hum īmānuhum" follows their faith when they saw the punishment of Allah.
